title: Regular-local acyclicity for a punctual finite free complex
statement: Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be a commutative regular local ring of finite Krull dimension $d\geq0$ [def-weil-regular-scheme]. Thus $R$ is Noetherian and local, and its maximal ideal can be generated by $d$ elements. Let $F^\bullet$ be a cochain complex of $R$-modules: its maps $d_F^i:F^i\to F^{i+1}$ satisfy $d_F^{i+1}d_F^i=0$, equivalently it is the chain complex with degree-$n$ term $F^{-n}$ [def-weil-pbc-module-chain-complex-homology]. Assume $F^i=0$ outside $0\leq i\leq d$, each $F^i$ finite free (having a finite basis) [def-weil-pbc-free-module]. Write $H^i(F)=\ker(d_F^i)/\operatorname{im}(d_F^{i-1})$. Assume that for every prime ideal $\mathfrak p\ne\mathfrak m$ of $R$ and every integer $i$, the localization $H^i(F)_{\mathfrak p}$ is zero (localization inverts all elements of $R\setminus\mathfrak p$). Then $H^i(F)=0$ for every $i<d$.

source.place: Tag 00N0, algebra-lemma-acyclic (Acyclicity lemma), specialized to finite free modules over a regular local ring and homology supported only at its maximal ideal. Also Mumford, Abelian Varieties, III §13, printed p.127, the displayed regular-local complex lemma; primary scan read at https://djvu.online/file/2tC7xp3dbqGCh.

proof.text: For $0\leq i\leq d$ set $C_i=F^i/\operatorname{im}(d_F^{i-1})$, with $C_0=F^0$. The complex identity gives a well-defined map $\delta_i:C_i\to F^{i+1}$, $[x]\mapsto d_F^i(x)$. Put $D_i=\operatorname{im}(\delta_i)$. Sending a cycle $z$ to its class $[z]\in C_i$ induces an injection $H^i(F)\hookrightarrow C_i$ with image $\ker(\delta_i)$: its kernel before passing to cohomology is exactly $\operatorname{im}(d_F^{i-1})$, and $\delta_i([z])=0$ means exactly $d_F^i(z)=0$. Hence $0\to H^i(F)\to C_i\to D_i\to0$ is short exact. Each $F^i$ is finite, generated by its finite basis. Images of finite generating sets generate their images and quotient modules, so $C_i$ and $D_i$ are finite. The kernel $H^i(F)\subset C_i$ is finite by the cited Noetherian-submodule lemma. All depth applications below are therefore to finite modules over the given Noetherian local ring.

source.place: Tag 00N0 (lemma-acyclic), breaking the complex into short exact sequences; Tag 00FP (lemma-Noetherian-finite-type-is-finite-presentation), part (2), for finiteness.

proof.text: Choose $x_1,\ldots,x_d$ generating $\mathfrak m$. The regular-parameter lemma makes this an $R$-regular sequence. For a nonzero finite free module $F^j\cong R^{r_j}$, $r_j>0$, its quotient by $(x_1,\ldots,x_c)$ is $(R/(x_1,\ldots,x_c))^{r_j}$ by taking basis coordinates. Multiplication by $x_{c+1}$ on this quotient is injective coordinate by coordinate, and the final quotient is $(R/\mathfrak m)^{r_j}\ne0$. Thus the same sequence is $F^j$-regular, and the definition of depth gives $\operatorname{depth}(F^j)\geq d$. For $F^j=0$ the depth is $\infty$, so the inequality still holds.

source.place: Tag 00NQ (lemma-regular-ring-CM); Tags 00LF (definition-regular-sequence) and 00LI (definition-depth); the finite-free case is the coordinatewise argument displayed here.

proof.text: If $i<0$, then $F^i=0$ and the formula for cohomology gives $H^i(F)=0$. When $d=0$ this already proves the conclusion. Assume $d>0$. We induct on $i=0,\ldots,d$ with invariant $\operatorname{depth}(C_i)\geq d-i$ and $H^j(F)=0$ for $0\leq j<i$. The base holds because $C_0=F^0$ and step 2 gives its depth bound.

source.place: Tag 00N0 (lemma-acyclic), induction along the complex, written in cochain order.

e0$, all three terms in that short exact sequence are nonzero; inequality (3) of the depth lemma gives $\operatorname{depth}(H^i(F))\geq\min\{\operatorname{depth}(C_i),\operatorname{depth}(D_i)+1\}\geq1$, since depth takes values in the nonnegative integers together with $\infty$. But the support of $H^i(F)$, defined as the primes with nonzero localization, is contained in $\{\mathfrak m\}$ by hypothesis. Every strictly increasing prime chain in this support has length at most zero. The depth/support-dimension bound, applied to the nonzero finite module $H^i(F)$, therefore gives $\operatorname{depth}(H^i(F))\leq\dim\operatorname{Supp}(H^i(F))\leq0$, a contradiction. Thus $H^i(F)=0$.

proof.text: Now $\ker(\delta_i)=H^i(F)=0$, and $\operatorname{im}(\delta_i)=\operatorname{im}(d_F^i)$ because $F^i\to C_i$ is surjective. Consequently $0\to C_i\xrightarrow{\delta_i}F^{i+1}\to C_{i+1}\to0$ is short exact. If $C_i=0$, then $C_{i+1}\cong F^{i+1}$, so its depth is at least $d\geq d-i-1$. If $C_{i+1}=0$, its depth is $\infty$. The case $F^{i+1}=0$ forces both other terms to be zero and is already covered. Otherwise all three terms are nonzero and inequality (2) of the depth lemma gives $\operatorname{depth}(C_{i+1})\geq\min\{\operatorname{depth}(F^{i+1}),\operatorname{depth}(C_i)-1\}\geq\min\{d,d-i-1\}=d-i-1$. Here $i<d$ makes the subtraction harmless, and $\infty-1=\infty$. Together with step 4 this establishes the invariant at $i+1$.

proof.text: Induction through $i=d-1$ gives $H^i(F)=0$ for $0\leq i<d$. Combined with the negative-degree computation in step 3, this is exactly the assertion for every integer $i<d$; no vanishing in degree $d$ has been used or asserted.
